Chapter 09

Your First MoQ System

On this page
Choose and record the implementationBefore running commandsUnderstand the path of one frameStart with the local demoCheck each boundaryAdd a second viewerTest a constrained networkTest a disconnectGoing beyond localhostSources and further reading

Let’s put a publisher, relay, and player together using the moq.dev local demo. We’ll start with its test video, add another viewer, then slow the network down to see what changes.

Before running it, we’ll look at the path one frame takes. As you work through the demo, keep notes on the version you’re using and what you see in the player and logs.

Choose and record the implementation

We’ll use the moq.dev project and its moq-lite and hang stack. The project’s documentation has the latest setup instructions; its standards guide explains which MOQT features it supports.

If you want to explore other stacks first, the MoQ Alliance getting-started guide lists demos, media tools, and transport libraries. Choose a publisher, relay, and player that agree on the protocol revision and media format.

The commands below follow the setup guide. Save the checkout revision and library versions with your notes so you can repeat the experiment later.

Run them from the moq.dev repository, not this book’s repository. They have not been executed as part of publishing this guide.

Before running commands

A terminal lets you start programs by typing commands. Your working directory is the folder those commands run in. git clone downloads a repository; cd moq enters that checkout. git rev-parse HEAD prints its current commit identifier, which lets another reader locate the same source revision. Git’s revision documentation explains that command.

The demo runs several processes: running programs with separate jobs. A listener accepts traffic at an address and port. localhost refers to the machine running the client, so opening a localhost address on your phone does not connect to the demo on your laptop.

Keep the terminal running while you use the demo. To stop the foreground recipe, press Ctrl+C in that terminal.

Understand the path of one frame

A source produces media. An encoder compresses it. The media layer supplies timing and configuration, and maps the encoded data into named tracks and groups. The publisher makes that content available through the relay.

The viewer chooses tracks, receives objects, interprets the media format, and decodes and presents the content. At each stage, ask what information is added and what can fail.

Once the demo is running, the observation table below will help you record the publication, transport, rendition, and codec.

Start with the local demo

This walkthrough follows the upstream quick start’s recommended Nix route, with flakes enabled. After installing that prerequisite, obtain the project and record the checkout you are using:

git clone https://github.com/moq-dev/moq
cd moq
git rev-parse HEAD
nix develop --command just

The documented default recipe runs a local relay, a test publisher, and the web demo. Follow the setup guide if your platform needs additional configuration. Use the supplied test content first, so a camera permission failure cannot be mistaken for a transport failure.

Save the revision printed by git rev-parse HEAD with your notes. The final command, nix develop --command just, opens the development environment and starts the demo.

For more detailed Rust logging, stop the demo and rerun it with the project’s documented logging setting:

RUST_LOG=debug nix develop --command just

The logs will vary with the version you’re running. Fill in what you can find below, and leave “not observed” for anything the player or logs don’t show.

Observation Your result
Project revision
Actual transport selected
Negotiated protocol and revision, if exposed
Broadcast/publication name
Selected media rendition
Codec and container, if exposed
Test video visible and audio audible

Watch the player alongside the relay logs. Follow the connection, discovery, and subscription messages through to the first picture and sound.

The moq.dev transport guide explains how its clients choose among transports. A browser exposing WebTransport does not prove the library selected it for this connection. Record what happened, including any fallback.

If you’re connecting different implementations, try a live subscription, a late join, and actual playback. Getting through version negotiation is just the first step; both sides also need the requests and media formats your app uses. The standards guide lists the project’s support.

Check each boundary

The quick start lists a local relay at localhost:4443 and a web demo at localhost:5173. If your checkout reports different addresses, use those.

Action Look for What you’ve checked
Start the recipe The relay, publisher, and web demo start without fatal errors The local processes launched
Open the web demo address The player interface loads The web server can serve the page
Select the test publication, if selection is offered Its media or track description becomes available The player found the publication
Start playback Pictures change over time; audio is audible when enabled At least one complete media path works
Inspect available logs Selected transport and accepted requests Which transport and request path produced that result

If the page loads but nothing plays, check the media connection next. If the video works but audio is silent, check mute and try clicking Play before investigating packet loss. Browsers may need a user action before playing audio; see MDN’s autoplay guide.

Add a second viewer

Open another viewer for the same publication. The relay now has more downstream work, while the original publication can be shared upstream. Inspect the relay’s metrics or logs instead of assuming the bandwidth pattern from the diagram alone.

Then close one viewer. Confirm that the other continues. Close both and observe whether the chosen publisher stops producing or transmitting the unused track. Demand-aware behavior depends on the application path and other subscribers, so record what actually happens.

Test a constrained network

Use a network test setup to constrain bandwidth or introduce delay. Start with one change at a time. Watch the selected rendition, playback age, audio continuity, and recovery after the constraint is removed.

Ordinary browser HTTP throttling tools may not shape every WebTransport path as expected. Verify that your chosen test tool affects the actual transport before drawing conclusions. Keep an unthrottled run as a baseline.

Watch what changes when the network slows down. Does the player choose a lower rendition, skip ahead, pause, or keep falling further behind? Compare that behavior with the unthrottled run.

Test a disconnect

Briefly disconnect the viewer, then restore its network access. Record whether the player reconnects by itself or requires a reload, how long it takes to show a new picture, and whether audio and video remain aligned. Compare this with the initial join: recovery may involve stale playback queues as well as a new session and subscriptions.

Going beyond localhost

Moving to another machine adds certificate trust, network reachability, and access policy. QUIC uses UDP; opening only a TCP listener does not establish its path. Follow the deployment guide for the listener and fallback configuration actually in use.

Do not add recording, multiple regions, and private user accounts simultaneously. Add one boundary, verify it, then continue. When something breaks, use the debugging chapter to find where data stops moving toward the player.
